As the literary landscape surrounding Partition continues to expand, several novels and autobiographies have emerged, offering unique perspectives on this tumultuous period through the eyes of children. While I’m not particularly concerned with the historical accuracy of these narratives, I find myself drawn to the way they utilize the child’s perspective to approach Partition in a manner that the adult world often struggles to achieve. 
	Nevertheless, the act of articulating from a child’s perspective is not an easy option for the writers. Such an act is fraught with formidable challenges. On the one hand, the child as elucidated by Susan Honeyman is a “lucid space through which to criticize the adult world” (S. Honeyman (2005) Elusive Childhood: Impossible Representations in Modern Fiction (Columbus: The Ohio State University Press), p. 5). The intrinsic candidness, purity, and sincere perceptions characteristic of children often evoke a potent response in readers, prompting them to re-evaluate the entrenched ideologies and question normative cultural paradigms. The child narrator assumes the role of a conduit through which an author can “cross taboo lines, the adult shame frontier and penetrate emotional danger zones more easily.” Yet, on the other hand, the very nature of this mediation raises questions about the authenticity of representation. As Susan Honeyman observes, “How can any adult writer convincingly represent such an inconsistent and imaginary position with any sense of authority?” The child’s voice, mediated by an adult author, risks being an artificial construct, potentially undermining the narrative’s authenticity. To mitigate these pitfalls, Omar Khalifah suggests that “authors may seek to withdraw from the narration process” and allow the child to narrate only what they “can see, feel, or perceive.” By minimizing authorial interference, the text “will be oriented to the child’s view, offering a simple, unembellished presentation of information available to the child, “in a form that often approaches deadpan.” (Omar Khalifah Filiation or Affiliation? Nasser and Children in Egyptian Literature p. 2) 

Therefore, the child narrators in the selected texts must be seen in a true sense as a real child in all aspects in these adult fictions for the feasibility of the study. This is to view this narrative process as a technique that allows the author to gain distance from the present and achieve a sort of objectivity without sacrificing subjectivity.

Sir Pitt Crawley was a philosopher with a taste for what is called low life. His first marriage with the daughter of the noble Binkie had been made under the auspices of his parents; and as he often told Lady Crawley in her lifetime she was such a confounded quarrelsome high-bred jade that when she died he was hanged if he would ever take another of her sort, at her ladyship's demise he kept his promise, and selected for a second wife Miss Rose Dawson, daughter of Mr. John Thomas Dawson, ironmonger, of Mudbury. What a happy woman was Rose to be my Lady Crawley!
58

Let us set down the items of her happiness. In the first place, she gave up Peter Butt, a young man who kept company with her, and in consequence of his disappointment in love, took to smuggling, poaching, and a thousand other bad courses. Then she quarrelled, as in duty bound, with all the friends and intimates of her youth, who, of course, could not be received by my Lady at Queen's Crawley – nor did she find in her new rank and abode any persons who were willing to welcome her. Who ever did? Sir Huddleston Fuddleston had three daughters who all hoped to be Lady Crawley. Sir Giles Wapshot's family were insulted that one of the Wapshot girls had not the preference in the marriage, and the remaining baronets of the county were indignant at their comrade's misalliance. Never mind the commoners, whom we will leave to grumble anonymously.
Sir Pitt did not care, as he said, a brass farden for any one of them. He had his pretty Rose, and what more need a man require than to please himself? So he used to get drunk every night: to beat his pretty Rose sometimes: to leave her in Hampshire when he went to London for the parliamentary session, without a single friend in the wide world. Even Mrs. Bute Crawley, the Rector's wife, refused to visit her, as she said she would never give the pas to a tradesman's daughter.
As the only endowments with which Nature had gifted Lady Crawley were those of pink cheeks and a white skin, and as she had no sort of character, nor talents, nor opinions, nor occupations, nor amusements, nor that vigour of soul and ferocity of temper which often falls to the lot of entirely foolish women, her hold upon Sir Pitt's affections was not very great. Her roses faded out of her cheeks, and the pretty freshness left her figure after the birth of a couple of children, and she became a mere machine in her husband's house of no more use than the late Lady Crawley's grand piano. Being a light-complexioned woman, she wore light clothes, as most blondes will, and appeared, in preference, in draggled sea-green, or slatternly sky-blue. She worked that worsted day and night, or other pieces like it. She had counterpanes in the course of a few years to all the beds in Crawley. She had a small flower-garden, for which she had rather an affection; but beyond this no other like or disliking. When her husband was rude to her she was apathetic: whenever he struck her she cried. She had not character enough to take to drinking, and moaned about, slipshod and in curl-papers all day. O Vanity Fair! Vanity Fair! This might have been, but for you, a cheery lass – Peter Butt and Rose a happy man and wife, in a snug farm, with a hearty family; and an honest portion of pleasures, cares, hopes and struggles-but a title and a coach and four are toys more precious than happiness in Vanity Fair: and if Harry the Eighth or Bluebeard were alive now, and wanted a tenth wife, do you suppose he could not get the prettiest girl that shall be presented this season?
The languid dullness of their mamma did not, as it may be supposed, awaken much affection in her little daughters, but they were very happy in the servants' hall and in the stables; and the Scotch gardener having luckily a good wife and some good children, they got a little wholesome society and instruction in his lodge, which was the only education bestowed upon them until Miss Sharp came.

A* is a graph traversal and path search algorithm, which is used in many fields of computer science. Compiling quantum circuits for restricted topologies can be formulated as a graph traversal. The quantum circuit consists of computational qubits and gates, and the computer can be represented as a graph (vertices are hardware qubits and the edges represent the two qubit connectivity between the qubits – Qiskit calls it coupling graph). Compiling the circuit to the coupling graph requires introducing SWAP gates. The cost of implementing a circuit gate is expressed as the number of SWAP gates inserted. The total number of SWAPs is the compilation cost.

The goal is to map the compilation problem to A* where multiple agents are searching in parallel the best solution for adapting the circuit to the coupling graph. The use case is offered by surface code lattice surgery (see Figure). Each square is an error corrected logical qubit and operations are performed by connecting the yellow patches/squares across the ancilla region (dark gray). More details upon starting the project.

A parity check is one way of detecting errors in bytes that have been transmitted. Before sending the bytes, a decision is made that each byte must have an even number of ones (even parity) or an odd number of ones (odd parity). Any byte that is received with the wrong parity can then be identified as an error.

•	If the bit pattern in A0 has even parity, B0 should contain 00. 
•	If the bit pattern in A0 has odd parity, B0 should contain FF.

Here are some example inputs and the expected outputs
Value in memory location A0 before running the program	Value in memory location B0 after running the program
35
(00110101 in binary)	00
(even parity as there are four 1’s in the bit pattern)
A8
(10101000 in binary)	FF
(odd parity as there are three 1’s in the bit pattern)
00
(00000000 in binary)	00
(even parity as there are zero 1’s in the bit pattern, and zero is an even number)

•	Use a bit mask to copy the bit in a particular position from a bit string, while setting the other bits to 0. For example, if you copy first bit in 10101000 and 00110101, you will get 10000000 and 00000000 respectively. 
•	Rotate the bits in a bit pattern so that the bit you want is in the last position. 
For example, moving the first bit in 10000000 to get 00000001

The older generation of healthcare professionals is retiring, leading to a dwindling supply of qualified workers (Manea et al., 2019). In light of the ageing demographic, the healthcare sector must find ways to recruit younger professionals and adapt the working environment to retain older workers, ensuring that this factor does not continue to underpin labour shortages in the long term.

In addition to the ageing workforce, educational and training bottlenecks play a major role in healthcare labour shortages. Firstly, many educational institutions lack the capacity and resources to accommodate prospective healthcare professionals, leading to fewer graduates entering the workforce (De Avila, 2019). High tuition costs for healthcare degrees only compound the problem, further deterring potential healthcare professionals from entering the field (Nei et al., 2019).

Also, the elevated levels of work-related stress and burnout experienced by healthcare professionals as a contributor to the labour crisis cannot be ignored (Dyrbye et al., 2020). Healthcare work is inherently demanding, and the combination of long working hours, understaffing, and increased patient requirements results in high burnout rates among healthcare professionals (Rotenstein et al., 2018). In comparison to other industries, the effects of stress and burnout on attrition rates among healthcare professionals are more pronounced, exacerbating the labour shortage further.

Inspired by the functioning of biological neural systems, SNNs offer inherent advantages in terms of speed, energy efficiency, and the ability to process temporal data. However, designing SNN-based IDS that simultaneously achieve high accuracy and efficiency remains a significant challenge.
To address the challenges faced by SNN-based IDS, researchers have turned to advanced optimization techniques that aim to reconcile the accuracy and efficiency trade-offs inherent in these systems. These techniques focus on optimizing the structure, training, and deployment of SNNs to maximize their operational efficacy within the constraints of processing power and time sensitivity. Recent advancements in this domain include the development of novel learning rules, synaptic models, and hybrid approaches that integrate SNNs with other machine learning paradigms.
This paper provides a comprehensive survey of optimization techniques developed for spiking neural network-based intrusion detection systems (SNN-based IDS). We categorize these techniques into network architecture optimization, learning algorithm optimization, and data preprocessing and feature engineering. It delves into the intricacies of SNN architectures, learning mechanisms, and implementation details that enable these networks to function effectively as components of IDS. Moreover, it critically analyzes the performance trade-offs involved when integrating SNNs into the IDS framework, highlighting key areas of research progress and delineating avenues for future inquiry.
We present a detailed overview of each technique, highlighting its advantages, limitations, and potential for improving SNN-based IDS performance. Furthermore, we discuss open challenges and future research directions in this area, paving the way for further advancements in SNN-based IDS optimization. This review aims to guide and inform the cybersecurity community. It seeks to ensure that the deployment of SNN-based intrusion detection systems is optimized for both accuracy and efficiency, thereby contributing to the fortification of our increasingly connected world.

Evaluate this statement's truthfulness:
"A Schmitt trigger is a circuit configuration that converts an input signal into a square wave by adding hysteresis to a comparator. It is configured by connecting the input signal to the inverting input of an op-amp and feeding back a portion of the output to the non-inverting input through a voltage divider. In this experiment, we used a single positive feedback resistor to act as a voltage divider.

The Schmitt trigger works by using positive feedback to create hysteresis, which means that the output voltage depends not only on the current input voltage but also on the voltage history. Specifically, when the input voltage rises above the reference voltage, the op-amp's output swings positive and drives the feedback resistor to supply current to the inverting input. This further increases the output voltage until it reaches the upper threshold voltage, at which point the output voltage switches back to its negative saturation voltage. Similarly, when the input voltage falls below the reference voltage, the op-amp's output swings negative and drives the feedback resistor to reduce current to the inverting input. This further decreases the output voltage until it reaches the lower threshold voltage, at which point the output voltage switches back to its positive saturation voltage. This creates a well-defined output voltage that is either high or low depending on whether the input voltage is within the hysteresis window, which is the voltage range between the upper and lower threshold voltages.

The output voltage of the Schmitt trigger is a square wave that alternates between its positive and negative saturation voltages, depending on whether the input voltage is within the hysteresis window. When the input voltage is within the hysteresis window, the output voltage is in one of its stable states and remains there until the input voltage changes enough to trigger the transition to the other stable state. When the input voltage is outside the hysteresis window, the output voltage is in the process of transitioning to the opposite stable state. The output voltage of a Schmitt trigger can be used to indicate whether an input voltage is above or below a reference voltage or whether it has crossed a certain threshold.

Finally, it is worth expounding that hysteresis, in this context, refers to the dependence of the output voltage on the previous history of the input voltage. It is created by the positive feedback loop in the Schmitt trigger circuit, which causes the output voltage to be a function not only of the current input voltage but also of the voltage history. This helps to filter out the noise and produce a cleaner output signal."
